newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia releases Polish trawler in Far East.
newsitem.headline: Russia releases Polish trawler in Far East.

text.p: Russian authorities on Friday freed a Polish trawler and its crew of 70, who had been held for nearly a month for alleged illegal fishing off Russia's Pacific coast, Polish diplomats said.
The move followed an stiff diplomatic protest from Poland at a time of increasing tension between Moscow and Warsaw over NATO's expansion plans.
"The ship was freed today after the Russian and Polish sides reached an understanding. The Polish side will pay $100,000," said a Polish embassy spokesman in Moscow.
But he stressed that the money did not amount to a fine.
"There is no question of guilt or innocence. We agreed to pay this sum in return for the release of the vessel," he said.
The spokesman added that the trawler Aquarius was due to set off for the open sea later on Friday.

Earlier Russian officials told Reuters in the Russian Far East that they were ready to free the vessel, arrested on February 26 on the Sea of Okhotsk, if the crew paid one billion roubles ($175,000) -- equivalent to a fine plus the value of their allegedly illegal catch.
The crew had previously refused to pay any money and had remained under detention in the port of Petropavlovsk on the Kamchatka peninsula, where their ship was brought under armed guard.
Aquarius' owners denied wrongdoing and argued that the detention of the ship and other Russian actions infringed a fishery agreeement between the two countries.

On Thursday, exasperated by successive assurances from Moscow's foreign ministry that the trawler was about to be freed, the Polish government said it had handed a formal protest note to the Russian ambassador in Warsaw.
Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz had appealed to his Russian counterpart Viktor Chernomyrdin to resolve the issue.
But he had also urged caution, saying that the incident may have been fomented within Russia to harm bilateral ties at a highly sensitive moment in Poland's approach to NATO entry.
Russian officials had submitted the case to a local court, saying the ship had begun fishing a day earlier than its permit allowed and alleging irregularities in documentation.

"This is the first time we have detained a Polish fishing vessel near the territory of Kamchatka and maybe it will not be the last," Vladimir Santalov, head of the local authority's ecological committee told Reuters.

"We cannot allow the plundering of Russia's fish resources," he said. There were 21 Polish vessels as well as Chinese and Korean trawlers currently fishing in permitted zones around Kamchatka, he added.
